analysis.one_liner: Requires food makers and importers to register, follow pathogen controls, face quarterly inspections, and recall contaminated food.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to a House committee and a health subcommittee and died there with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put the federal government in charge of a national food safety program for FDA-regulated foods. Every food processing facility and importer would have to register, follow sanitation and process-control rules, keep records, and open its doors to unannounced inspections at least four times a year. The government could set contamination limits, mandate recalls of dangerous food, trace products to their source, fine violators up to $100,000 per violation, and protect employees who report problems. It also would have funded public education about food safety and research into contamination.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats food regulated by the FDA — essentially all consumers, since the bill targets bacteria, chemicals, toxins, viruses, and parasites in the food supply. Children, the elderly, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems are named as groups whose risks must be specifically analyzed when contamination limits are set [S3]. Workers who blow the whistle on unsafe food handling would gain new legal protection against retaliation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires food processing facilities and importers to register with the Secretary of Health and Human Services and to adopt process controls, sanitation standards, recordkeeping, and sampling designed to limit human pathogens and other harmful substances in food [S2] [S3].

Facilities and importers would face unannounced inspections at least quarterly, with waivers only for facilities the Secretary certifies as exceptional or negligible-risk based on their products and compliance history [S2] [S3].
The Secretary could set science-based tolerances for contaminants, with risks to sensitive groups such as children, the elderly, pregnant women, and the immune-compromised specifically analyzed [S3].

When food poses a reasonable probability of a public health threat, the Secretary could first order ceasing distribution and consumer notice, and after a hearing within two days, issue a mandatory recall — powers that did not then exist for FDA-regulated foods [S2] [S3].

The bill adds civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation (each day a violation continues counts separately), a citizen suit mechanism, mandatory whistleblower protection for food-safety complainants, and a rigorous inspection system for imported food, including certification of exporting nations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food processors and importers regulated by the FDA, who would bear the cost of registration, upgraded process controls, recordkeeping, sampling, and quarterly inspections, and could face civil fines up to $100,000 per violation per day. The federal government (taxpayers) would fund the inspection workforce, surveillance, research, and a public education program, with 'such sums as may be necessary' authorized for two fiscal years [S3].

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden would fall hardest on smaller food processors: mandatory registration, recordkeeping, sampling, and quarterly inspections cost money regardless of facility size, and the bill sets no explicit small-business accommodations (the Secretary could exempt only classes of facilities from registration) [S3].

The inspection mandate is expensive and potentially duplicative: quarterly unannounced inspections of every registered facility would require a large expansion of federal inspectors, funded by an open-ended 'such sums as may be necessary' appropriation with no cost estimate provided [S3].

Penalties and suspension of registration are potent: a facility's registration can be suspended immediately for refusing inspection or for violations the Secretary deems risky, and judicial review of penalties is limited to a court of appeals, which industry would likely argue denies facilities a full day in district court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: at the time, FDA-regulated food facilities were inspected infrequently and the agency lacked mandatory recall authority. The consumer protections are strong and the cost falls mostly on the industry responsible for contamination and on federal budgets. The main design weakness is the open-ended, unfunded inspection and paperwork burden, which could squeeze small processors without proportionate safety gains. On balance, the benefits to public health plausibly outweigh the compliance costs, but the bill never got the hearing process where such trade-offs would have been worked out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health subcommittee, and stayed there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and not even a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-NJ) introduced the Consumer Food Safety Act of 2001 on May 10, 2001 [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on May 22, 2001 to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never left committee before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: FDA-regulated food processors and importers avoided new registration, inspection, recordkeeping, recall, and penalty requirements, since no committee or floor action ever took place. Consumers gained nothing; the food safety gaps the bill targeted remained until later legislation in a future Congress.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 10, 2001 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 22, 2001 and took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan alignment — only an absence of support anywhere [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed registration, quarterly unannounced inspections, process controls, recordkeeping, sampling, traceability, and civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation per day on an industry that at the time faced infrequent FDA oversight and no mandatory recall authority. Its interest in avoiding these costs ran against consumers' interest in safer food.

Recall and notification orders under the bill would reach distributors and retailers, adding compliance duties, but mandatory recalls could also protect them from selling contaminated products and from the reputational damage of outbreaks.

Imported food would face intensified inspections unless the exporting nation was certified as providing equivalent protection, and unsafe imports could be impounded and condemned at the port. This aligns with consumers' interest in safe imports but would raise costs for exporters.
